lines.raw: The crabs' fit came from an algorithm built on one idea: pretend you know what you don't. <bookmark mark='a'/> We observe each crab's ratio. <bookmark mark='b'/> We don't observe which race it belongs to, if races there are. <bookmark mark='c'/> The likelihood of what we did observe is a log of a sum, one term per component, and setting its derivatives to zero gives equations nobody can solve by hand. <bookmark mark='d'/> But if the labels were known, the complete-data log likelihood would be a sum of logs: the proportion would be the share of race one, and each component's mean and spread would be the ordinary mean and spread of its own crabs.
lines.spoken: The crabs' fit came from an algorithm built on one idea: pretend you know what you don't. We observe each crab's ratio. We don't observe which race it belongs to, if races there are. The likelihood of what we did observe is a log of a sum, one term per component, and setting its derivatives to zero gives equations nobody can solve by hand. But if the labels were known, the complete-data log likelihood would be a sum of logs: the proportion would be the share of race one, and each component's mean and spread would be the ordinary mean and spread of its own crabs.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> So alternate. In the E-step, for expectation, use the current parameters to compute each crab's probability of belonging to race one: its responsibility. <bookmark mark='b'/> In the M-step, for maximization, refit as if the responsibilities were labels: the proportion is the average responsibility, and each mean and variance is a weighted mean and variance. <bookmark mark='c'/> Monitor likelihood changes, parameter changes and numerical diagnostics; a tiny likelihood increment alone need not establish parameter accuracy. <bookmark mark='d'/> Arthur Dempster, Nan Laird and Donald Rubin named the algorithm in 1977 and gave a general framework for many incomplete-data problems, although either step may still be difficult; special cases go back to the epidemiologist Anderson McKendrick in 1926 and to the Baum–Welch algorithm for hidden Markov models.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Here's the E-step at the final fit, on Weldon's histogram. <bookmark mark='b'/> Each interval's crabs are split between the races in proportion to their responsibilities: blue is the expected number from race one, <bookmark mark='c'/> red the expected number from race two. Almost every crab on the far left is blue; <bookmark mark='d'/> just left of the histogram's peak, at point six five three five, about a fifth are still blue, and in the far right tail blue creeps back, because race one is the broader. <bookmark mark='e'/> No crab is ever assigned outright; EM splits each one and fits the pieces.

lines.raw: Why does it work? <bookmark mark='a'/> Write the likelihood as a sum over the unseen labels, and multiply and divide by any distribution q for those labels. <bookmark mark='b'/> The log is concave, so by Jensen's inequality the log of an average is at least the average of the logs: a lower bound on the log likelihood. <bookmark mark='c'/> The bound is tight, equal, when q is the conditional distribution of the labels given the data at the current parameters, which is exactly what the E-step computes. <bookmark mark='d'/> So the E-step builds a lower bound that touches the log likelihood at the current point. Q is the expected complete-data log likelihood, and the M-step maximizes it.

The bound is tight, equal, when q is the conditional distribution of the labels given the data at the current parameters, which is exactly what the E-step computes. So the E-step builds a lower bound that touches the log likelihood at the current point. Q is the expected complete-data log likelihood, and the M-step maximizes it.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Here's that picture along one coordinate, the mixing proportion, with the other four held at their estimates. The green curve is the log likelihood. <bookmark mark='b'/> Start at p equals point nine. The E-step builds the gold lower bound, touching the curve there. <bookmark mark='c'/> The M-step jumps to the bound's peak, and since the bound lies below the curve, the curve there is at least as high. <bookmark mark='d'/> Build a new bound at the new point, jump again, and again. <bookmark mark='e'/> Every step climbs. This is the minorize-maximize idea of Part 21, with the bound supplied by the missing data.
lines.spoken: Here's that picture along one coordinate, the mixing proportion, with the other four held at their estimates. The green curve is the log likelihood. Start at p equals point nine. The E-step builds the gold lower bound, touching the curve there. The M-step jumps to the bound's peak, and since the bound lies below the curve, the curve there is at least as high. Build a new bound at the new point, jump again, and again. Every step climbs. This is the minorize-maximize idea of Part 21, with the bound supplied by the missing data.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> The full five-parameter run on the crabs started from p equals one half and ended at point four three. <bookmark mark='b'/> It took one thousand six hundred and twenty-two iterations. <bookmark mark='c'/> On a log scale, the gap between the current log likelihood and the attained local log-likelihood limit falls approximately along a straight line: linear convergence, the same fraction of the error gone each step. <bookmark mark='d'/> Here each step keeps ninety-nine point three six percent of the error in the parameters, so the gap, which is quadratic in the error, shrinks by about one point three percent per step. <bookmark mark='e'/> Newton's method from Part 21 would finish in a handful of steps, but unsafeguarded Newton can wander off or propose a negative variance. EM preserves nonnegative variance updates, yet can still approach a singular collapsed component. Practical software often runs EM first and finishes with Newton.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Near a regular isolated EM fixed point, the dominant linear convergence rate is an eigenvalue of the missing-information fraction matrix. Our successive-step estimate illustrates that local result. <bookmark mark='b'/> Thomas Louis turned this into a formula for standard errors in 1982: the observed information is the complete information minus the missing information. <bookmark mark='c'/> For the crabs the rate is point nine nine three six: the two races overlap so much that the labels, which would make the problem easy, are almost entirely unknown. <bookmark mark='d'/> The observed information gives a standard error for the proportion of point one five, so the local curvature approximation is forty-three percent plus or minus twenty-nine points. Weak separation and mixture irregularity limit the reliability of this Wald approximation. The means are pinned down to a few thousandths, but how the crabs divide between the races the data barely say.
